\begin{abstract}
Most work on telling large language models apart uses English, and the accuracy that interpretable features give up against character $n$-grams has not been measured on multilingual data with the content held fixed. We collected \NCollected{} persuasive essays from five frontier models in seven languages, using \NPrompts{} prompts with the same content in every language, and described each essay with \NFeatures{} features computed the same way from Universal Dependencies parses. Under leave-one-prompt-out cross-validation, logistic regression on these features identifies the author with \LRmin{}--\LRmax{}\% accuracy in every language (chance is \Chance{}), and most of that accuracy holds for a reading-level instruction the classifier never saw. Character $n$-grams are \GapNGmin{} to \GapNGmax{} points more accurate within a language, but with the same unlabeled adaptation the features transfer better between languages (\TransferOff{}\% against \NGFairOff{}\%). We detect no decline in lower-resource languages, though a drop of up to \SteepestDeclinePts{} points cannot be ruled out. The signal survives machine translation, while the five models themselves name the author at close to chance (\JudgeMin{}--\JudgeMax{}\%). In this setting (one genre, a fixed prompt set and one sampling temperature), the author of non-English machine text can be identified from features a person can inspect.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
authorship attribution, AI-generated text, multilingual text mining, interpretable features, large language models
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Most work on machine-generated text asks whether a person or a model wrote a text. Provenance also asks which model wrote it, and most of what we know about that comes from English~\cite{uchendu2020authorship,sun2025idiosyncrasies}. The two multilingual studies we know of use fine-tuned or probability-based classifiers~\cite{lacava2026multilingual,greco2026multighost}, which give no reason for a decision. A moderator tracing a coordinated campaign in Hindi, or a teacher checking a Turkish essay, can act on ``this text uses paragraphs and punctuation the way model A does'' more easily than on a score from a classifier they cannot inspect, and fine-tuned detectors for each language and model version rarely exist outside English.

There are two reasons to doubt that English results carry over. Models see less training text in lower-resource languages~\cite{joshi2020state}, so their writing there may be less distinctive, and many stylometric measures are undefined outside English or track the language more than the author. Character $n$-grams, the most successful single feature type in authorship attribution~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}, work in any language but are tied to the script and vocabulary they were trained on.

We study five frontier models in seven languages, hold each essay's content fixed across languages, and describe every text with \NFeatures{} features computed the same way from Universal Dependencies (UD) parses~\cite{nivre2020ud}. An analysis plan committed before data collection (Sec.~\ref{sec:analysis}) asks whether the models can be told apart within each language (\textbf{RQ1}), whether attribution weakens as a language's resource level falls (\textbf{RQ2}), whether a model's style carries across languages (\textbf{RQ3}) and whether the models converge in lower-resource languages (\textbf{RQ4}). Whether machine translation removes the signal (\textbf{RQ5}) and whether the models can identify the author themselves (\textbf{RQ6}) were added before their data were collected, and the $n$-gram baseline, feature-economy analysis and robustness checks came later. Table~\ref{tab:summary} answers each question in one line and says when each representation is the better choice.

\section{Related Work}
\textbf{Detection and stylometry.} Human-versus-machine detectors fine-tuned on English lose about a quarter of their F1 on other languages~\cite{macko2023multitude}. For human authors, character $n$-grams are the most successful single feature~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}, masking all but the most frequent words isolates a structural signal~\cite{stamatatos2017distortion}, and UD-derived syntactic features attribute authors in several languages~\cite{gorman2022ud}.

\textbf{Model attribution.} In English, attribution among neural generators~\cite{uchendu2020authorship} has used stylometric features~\cite{kumarage2023neural} and embedding classifiers, and Sun et al.\ show that the latter separate model families and largely survive LLM translation into Chinese~\cite{sun2025idiosyncrasies}. Models optimized to fool detectors still keep a distinct style~\cite{riverasoto2026attacks}. Multilingual work relies on fine-tuned or probability-based detectors. La Cava et al.\ cover seven older LLMs and human text in 18 languages and find generators harder to tell apart in English~\cite{lacava2026multilingual}, and MultiGhostBench covers five recent LLMs in six languages~\cite{greco2026multighost}. Zaitsu et al.\ attribute Japanese text among six LLMs with part-of-speech and function-word features~\cite{zaitsu2026fingerprint}. To our knowledge, no earlier study of which model wrote a text uses one feature set with the same definition in every language, holds content fixed across languages, and compares it with character $n$-grams under matched adaptation.

\textbf{Homogenization and LLM judges.} Writing with LLMs reduces the diversity of human text~\cite{padmakumar2024diversity}, but whether models converge on each other as training data thins has not been tested. LLM evaluators favor their own outputs~\cite{panickssery2024self}, and models asked to name the author of a single English text score near chance and default to GPT or Claude~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition}. RQ6 repeats that task in seven languages.

\section{Data and Method}
\subsection{Models, Languages and Prompts}
We queried the five subject models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok 4.3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro) through OpenRouter in September 2026 and logged the served model identifier of every response. The seven languages are English, Spanish, Chinese, Russian, Japanese, Turkish and Hindi. Before data collection we gave them resource ranks 1 to 7 in that order, as a rough proxy for their share of web training data. The ranking is open to dispute: Joshi et al.~\cite{joshi2020state} put English, Spanish, Chinese and Japanese in their highest class (5) and Russian, Turkish and Hindi one class lower (4), so we also report that two-class split.

Twelve English prompt schemas each fix a topic, a stance (six for, six against), three supporting claims, a prose-only instruction and a reading level (four prompts each for general, educated and expert readers). For each language, a model that is not a subject (Llama 4 Maverick) wrote a native prompt from the schema rather than translating the English one, so the wording is idiomatic while the content stays the same. A model from a third family (Qwen 3.7 Plus) read each of the 84 prompts blind, extracted the topic, stance and claims, and compared them with the schema. Prompts that failed were regenerated with the reviewer's note until all 84 passed.

\subsection{Generation, Validation and Features}
Each prompt was sent as a single user turn with no system prompt, at temperature 0.7, twice per cell with fixed seeds and with hidden reasoning excluded, giving $5 \times \NPrompts{} \times 7 \times 2 = \NCollected{}$ responses. Each response had to pass language identification (confidence $\geq 0.6$), fall within 150 to 900 word equivalents and pass a per-language refusal check. One Grok response to a Hindi prompt was in English and was excluded, leaving \NResponses{} texts, and ten DeepSeek responses that used up their token budget on hidden reasoning were collected again with a larger budget.

We parsed the texts with Stanza~\cite{qi2020stanza}, splitting Chinese and Japanese on sentence-final punctuation first, and computed \NFeatures{} features in five groups. \emph{Lexical}: moving-average type-token ratio (MATTR, window 50), hapax rate, mean token length, Zipf slope. \emph{Syntactic}: mean and SD of sentence length, burstiness of sentence length, mean maximum dependency depth, subordinate clauses per sentence (\texttt{acl}, \texttt{advcl}, \texttt{ccomp}, \texttt{xcomp}, \texttt{csubj}), function-word ratio, first-person rate. \emph{Structure}: paragraph count and length, question rate, connective rate. \emph{Punctuation}: commas, colons, dashes and semicolons per 1,000 tokens, with full-width and script-specific variants mapped to the same feature. \emph{Character}: character-bigram entropy and digit rate.

\subsection{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}
The analysis plan (\texttt{docs/analysis\_plan.md}) was committed on 3 September 2026 (commit \texttt{82673ac}) before any response was collected, and the repository and its history are public. RQ5 was added before any translation existed (\texttt{88e08a7}). RQ6 was added before the judge data were collected, after a small pilot that set the reasoning condition (\texttt{60593f5}, \texttt{c7232ff}).

\textbf{Validation and tests.} The two generations of a prompt are related, and so are its versions in the seven languages. Every split is therefore leave-one-prompt-out (LOPO, \NPrompts{} folds), every interval is a prompt-clustered bootstrap, the GLMs use prompt-clustered errors, and accuracy differences are tested on the \NPrompts{} per-prompt accuracies with an exact sign-flip permutation test (4,096 sign assignments; the smallest one-sided $p$ is \PLMinP{}). Holm correction is applied over the 28 headline comparisons (features and $n$-grams against chance, features against $n$-grams, and features against the best judge, in seven languages), over the 42 transfer pairs of each representation and over the five judges. Spearman $p$-values over seven languages are exact.

\textbf{Classifiers and tuning.} Features are standardized inside each training fold (no feature has missing values) and fed to $L_2$-regularized multinomial logistic regression. The baseline fits TF-IDF over character 1--4-grams within word boundaries (minimum document frequency 2, sublinear term frequency, at most 60,000 terms) on the training prompts only, followed by the same classifier; word 1--2-grams are handled the same way. The features use $C = 1$, as fixed in the plan, and the later $n$-gram baseline uses the same $C$ with TF-IDF settings that were set once and not tuned. As a check, we also choose $C \in \{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100\}$ for both by nested LOPO on the training prompts.

\textbf{RQ2.} A binomial GLM of cell-level correctness on resource rank, with errors clustered by prompt, by language, and by both. \textbf{RQ3.} A per-feature ANOVA (model $\times$ language, with prompt as a block) gives partial $\eta^2$. For transfer, features are z-scored within each language (using all texts of that language, without labels) and a classifier trained on language $A$ is tested on language $B$. The $n$-gram version fits the vocabulary on the union of $A$ and $B$ without labels and z-scores the TF-IDF columns within each language, so both representations get the same unlabeled adaptation. \textbf{RQ4.} After within-language z-scoring, we compute the mean pairwise distance between the five model centroids, the silhouette of the model labels and the between/within scatter ratio. \textbf{RQ5.} Google Translate and an open non-subject model (MiniMax M3) translated all 120 English responses into the other six languages. We measure attribution on the translations, transfer from classifiers trained on the English originals or on native target-language responses, and each feature's Spearman correlation between originals and translations. \textbf{RQ6.} Each subject model saw one text at a time, with a shuffled candidate list and no metadata, and was asked which of the five models wrote it (temperature 0, hidden reasoning off where possible), the exact-model task of Bai et al.~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition}. \textbf{Feature economy.} A nested selection curve (features ranked by mean absolute standardized coefficient on the training fold only, then the top $k$ refit), group ablations, and a character model that sees only punctuation, digits and whitespace~\cite{stamatatos2017distortion}. \textbf{Fragility.} We train on the eight prompts of two reading levels and test on the four prompts of the third, and we rerun LOPO without the two paragraph features.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Within-Language Attribution}
Table~\ref{tab:main} shows that the features identify the author in every language, with accuracy between \LRmin{}\% (Turkish) and \LRmax{}\% (English) against \Chance{} chance. Every prompt-clustered interval excludes chance, and in all seven languages the prompt-level test against chance has Holm $p \leq \PLChanceHolmMax{}$. Part of the signal is length. When each feature is residualized on log length within a language, accuracy falls to \LRlenMin{}--\LRlenMax{}\%, which is still well above chance.

\textbf{$n$-gram baseline.} Character $n$-grams are more accurate, at \NGmin{}--\NGmax{}\%, or \GapNGmin{} to \GapNGmax{} points above the features (\GapNGmean{} on average). They lead in \PLNGFavMin{} to \PLNGFavMax{} of the 12 prompts in every language except English (\PLNGFavEn{}), but with 12 prompts the difference is Holm-significant only in \PLNGsigLangs{} (\PLNGNextLang{} is next, at $p = \PLNGNextHolm{}$). Choosing $C$ for both by nested LOPO (selected values \TunedFeatC{} for the features, \TunedNGC{} for $n$-grams) moves mean accuracy \TunedFeatMeanChange{} for the features and \TunedNGMeanChange{} for $n$-grams, widening the gap to \TunedGapMin{}--\TunedGapMax{} points (mean \TunedGapMean{}), so the default settings do not favor the features. As expected~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}, $n$-grams gain from vocabulary and morphology that the features leave out.

\textbf{Fragility.} Trained on prompts with two of the three reading levels and tested on prompts with the third, the features reach \LOTOFeatMin{}--\LOTOFeatMax{}\% ($\LOTOFeatChange{}$ points from LOPO on average) and $n$-grams reach \LOTONGMin{}--\LOTONGMax{}\% ($\LOTONGChange{}$ points). Without the two paragraph features, which a layout instruction would change first, the features reach \NoParaMin{}--\NoParaMax{}\% under LOPO and \LOTONoParaMin{}--\LOTONoParaMax{}\% across reading levels, and every prompt-clustered interval stays above chance (the lowest bound is \LOTONoParaCIminLo{}\%). We did not vary format instructions or temperature.

\textbf{LLM judges (RQ6).} Asked which of the five models wrote a single text, the judges score between \Judgedeepseek{} (DeepSeek) and \Judgeclaude{} (Claude). Only Claude is above chance (on all \PLClaudePrompts{} prompts; Holm over the five judges $p = \PLClaudeHolm{}$, next judge $p = \PLOtherJudgesHolmMin{}$), and only Claude names itself more often for its own texts than for others' (\JudgeclaudeOwn{} against \JudgeclaudeFalse{}; \PLClaudeSelfPrompts{} of 12 prompts, $p = \PLClaudeSelfHolm{}$). GPT-5.5 names itself for \JudgegptSelfClaim{} of texts whoever wrote them. The feature classifier beats the best judge by \GapJudgeMin{} to \GapJudgeMax{} points in every language (Holm $p \leq \PLJudgeHolmMax{}$). Bai et al.~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition} found the same near-chance behavior, biased toward GPT and Claude, in English, and we see it in every language except for Claude in Hindi (\JudgeBesthi{}\%).

\subsection{Feature Importance}
\label{sec:economy}
Ranked by mean absolute standardized coefficient, the strongest features are \TopCoefFeatures{}. Language explains far more of each feature's variance than the model does (mean partial $\eta^2$ of \EtaLang{} against \EtaModel{}, with \EtaInter{} for the interaction and \EtaPrompt{} for the prompt). Model effects are largest for \EtaModelTopFive{} and smallest for subordination, question rate and dependency depth ($\leq \EtaModelSmallMax{}$), so the models differ mainly in lexical variety, punctuation and paragraphing and very little in clause structure.

A few features do most of the work (Fig.~\ref{fig:feat}a). The five features ranked highest on the training folds reach \CurveKfiveShareMin{}--\CurveKfiveShareMax{}\% of the full set's macro-F1 (\CurveKfiveMin{}--\CurveKfiveMax{} against \CurveKtwentyoneMin{}--\CurveKtwentyoneMax{}). The ranking depends on the language: paragraph count is \ParaCountRankRu{} in Russian but \ParaCountRankEn{} in English. Pooled over languages, the order is \PooledTopFive{}. No group of features is essential: removing any one group costs at most \AblMaxDrop{} macro-F1 (\AblMaxDropWhere{}). A character model that sees only punctuation, digits and whitespace reaches \PunctDiagMin{}--\PunctDiagMax{}\% within a language, so segmentation, punctuation and length carry a signal of their own.

\subsection{Transfer and Translation}
\label{sec:transfer}
\textbf{Cross-language transfer (RQ3).} Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}a shows that a classifier trained in one language and tested in another, after z-scoring the features within each language, reaches \TransferMin{}--\TransferMax{}\% (\TransferOff{}\% on average, against \TransferDiag{}\% within a language). All 42 pairs are above chance at the prompt level after Holm correction ($p \leq \PLTransferHolmMax{}$). Character $n$-grams given the same unlabeled adaptation average \NGFairOff{}\% (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}b) and are significantly above chance in \PLTransferNGSig{} of the 42 pairs. The features do better in \FeatBeatsNGCells{} pairs and on all \PLTransferPairPrompts{} prompts (paired sign-flip $p = \PLTransferPairP{}$). Without adaptation, $n$-grams transfer at \NGTransferOff{}\%. Since the test language contains the \NPrompts{} training prompts, these are upper bounds for unseen prompts.

\textbf{Translation (RQ5).} Classifiers trained and tested on the translations (LOPO) reach \TrAllMin{}--\TrAllMax{}\%, about \TrCostPts{} points below the English originals and close to native responses in the same languages (\TrNativeMean{}\% on average), and every prompt-clustered interval excludes chance (lowest bound \PLTrMinLo{}\%). Paragraph count ($\rho = \Survparacount{}$), paragraph length (\Survparalenmean{}), digit rate (\Survdigitrate{}) and sentence length (\Survsentlenmean{}) survive mostly by construction (Fig.~\ref{fig:feat}b), because both translators keep paragraph and sentence boundaries and copy digits, while MATTR (\Survmattr{}), function-word ratio (\Survfuncwordratio{}) and bigram entropy (\Survbigramentropy{}) are largely set by the target language. A classifier trained on native target-language responses, which has seen none of these texts, scores \TrGoogleTrainNative{}\% (Google) and \TrLLMTrainNative{}\% (LLM) on average. An English-trained $n$-gram model without vocabulary adaptation scores \NGTrTrainEnNonEsMin{}--\NGTrTrainEnNonEsMax{}\% on every target language except Spanish, and Turkish, which also uses the Latin script, is no exception, so the loss comes from vocabulary rather than script.

\subsection{Resource Gradient and Convergence}
\textbf{Resource gradient (RQ2).} We find no decline along the resource ranking. The cell-level GLM gives $\beta = \Beta{}$ log-odds per step (SE \BetaSE{}, 95\% CI $\BetaLo{}$ to $\BetaHi{}$; \BetaP{} clustered by prompt, \BetaLangP{} by language with seven clusters, \BetaLangPromptP{} by both), less than one accuracy point per step, and the order is not monotone (Hindi is above Spanish and Turkish). The test has limited power, however: the minimum detectable effect at 80\% power is about \MDEpts{} points over the six steps, and the interval allows a decline of up to \SteepestDeclinePts{}, so we cannot conclude that accuracy is unchanged. Joshi et al.'s classes give the same picture (\ClassFiveMean{}\% for Class 5, \ClassFourMean{}\% for Class 4), as does the $n$-gram baseline (Hindi \NGhi{}\%, English \NGen{}\%; GLM \NGglmP{}).

\textbf{Convergence (RQ4).} The models do not meet the convergence rule in the plan. The mean centroid distance falls from \CentEn{} $z$-units in English to \CentHi{} in Hindi ($\rho = \CentRho{}$ against rank, \CentPexact{}; prompt-clustered intervals [\PCCentEnLo{}, \PCCentEnHi{}] and [\PCCentHiLo{}, \PCCentHiHi{}]). The between/within scatter ratio falls from \BWen{} to \BWhi{} ($\rho = \BWrho{}$, \BWPexact{}), but its intervals overlap ([\PCBWEnLo{}, \PCBWEnHi{}] and [\PCBWHiLo{}, \PCBWHiHi{}]), and the silhouette stays between $\SilMin{}$ and $\SilMax{}$, while the rule requires all three to separate. Most of the drop from English to Hindi comes from Grok, whose four pairs fall from a mean distance of \GrokPairsEn{} to \GrokPairsHi{}, while the other six pairs average \OtherPairsEn{} in English and \OtherPairsHi{} in Hindi ($\rho = \OtherPairsRho{}$ against rank, \OtherPairsPexact{}). The decline reflects one model rather than general convergence, and neither this result nor La Cava et al.'s~\cite{lacava2026multilingual} supports a convergence claim.

\section{Discussion}
Within this setting, interpretable attribution works outside English, and a classifier trained in one language transfers to the others after unlabeled standardization. Table~\ref{tab:summary} summarizes when to use which representation: character $n$-grams when labeled texts in the target language exist and no explanation is needed, and the features when a decision has to be explained or applied in another language. Neither method can attribute a text to a model outside the candidate set, and we did not test translation combined with a paraphrase attack~\cite{riverasoto2026attacks}.

\textbf{Dual use.} The features also apply to human text, but UD-derived features are already used to attribute human authors~\cite{gorman2022ud}, so the release adds a method rather than a new capability. Pseudonymous writers should note that translation did not hide the author here. We release model-generated text only.

\textbf{Limitations.} The study covers one genre, persuasive essays with three fixed claims and no lists, so paragraph count and length partly record how each model lays out an argument, and both translators keep paragraph boundaries. All texts were sampled at temperature 0.7 without a system prompt, from model versions served in one month, and we varied the reading-level instruction but not format instructions or temperature; a prompt that dictates the layout could weaken the strongest single cue. Length is entangled with style and is not controlled in the transfer, convergence and translation analyses, and the resource ranking is coarse. Eight features depend on Stanza parses or sentence splitting, whose accuracy varies by language without following the resource order~\cite{qi2020stanza}, although four of the five top pooled features need no parser. The transfer and translation tests reuse the same \NPrompts{} prompts, which also limit the power of the prompt-level tests, and a model, not native speakers, checked prompt fidelity. All five subjects are closed APIs; we did not test open-weight models, adversarial rewriting or a fine-tuned multilingual encoder~\cite{greco2026multighost}, and the judges saw one text at a time without extended reasoning.

\section{Conclusion}
In this setting, \NFeatures{} interpretable features with one definition in every language identify which of five frontier LLMs wrote a persuasive essay, in seven languages, with \LRmin{}--\LRmax{}\% accuracy. Character $n$-grams are more accurate within a language, but the features transfer better between languages. Most of the signal comes from a few features, led in the pooled ranking by paragraph count and length, that pass through translation almost unchanged, and it holds for an unseen reading-level instruction and without the paragraph features. Next we will test other genres, format instructions and temperatures, have native speakers check the prompts, and add a multilingual encoder baseline.
